title: Beyond LEO Fire Audit: evidence and verdicts
note: Evidence records were drafted with an AI model from the cited documents and checked against them. Verdicts are computed by fixed rules. Screening estimates only.

environments.name: ISS
environments.notes: Sea-level air. Volume is the NASA pressurized volume of 1,005 m³; the habitable volume is 388 m³.

environments.name: Orion-class capsule
environments.notes: Volume is the 330 cubic feet of habitable volume NASA lists for Orion; its pressurized volume is 690.6 cubic feet (19.6 m³). Sea-level air is assumed here. Orion was designed for up to 30% oxygen at 10.2 psia, and its materials are certified at that condition.

environments.name: Lunar lander or habitat
environments.notes: NASA states that the lander, lunar habitat and pressurized rover nominally use 8.2 psia (56.5 kPa) with 34% oxygen. The 17 m³ volume is an assumption, set to match the free volume in which Saffire measured toxic gases.

environments.name: Pressurized rover
environments.notes: Same nominal atmosphere as the lander. Volume is the 13 m³ living space of the JAXA and Toyota pressurized rover concept.

environments.name: Mars surface habitat
environments.notes: Gravity is 0.38 g. The atmosphere is assumed equal to the lunar exploration atmosphere and the 100 m³ volume is a placeholder. Change both in the cabin builder.

rules.rule: A material that passes the 1 g flame test is safe to fly
rules.issPractice: NASA screens cabin materials with an upward-burning test in normal gravity, NASA-STD-6001 Test 1. A sample that burns more than 15 cm fails.
rules.verdictRule: Weakens at 0 g, where orbit data show lower oxygen limits. Breaks in partial gravity, where ground tests show materials burning below their 1 g limit.

rules.rule: The smoke detector responds to smoke from any likely fuel
rules.issPractice: ISS uses laser light-scattering detectors. They respond best to particles above about 1 µm and reach down to about 0.6 µm.
rules.verdictRule: Weakens everywhere. Orbit tests show the ISS detector missing smoke from two common wire and insulation plastics.

rules.rule: An alarm means fire, not dust
rules.issPractice: A light-scattering detector reacts to any particle of the right size. DAFT found ISS cabin air substantially cleaner than the Shuttle or a typical office.
rules.verdictRule: Weakens in any cabin, because ISS crews already see nuisance alarms from dust. Breaks where planetary dust enters the cabin.

rules.rule: Cabin airflow carries the smoke to the detectors
rules.issPractice: With no up or down, ISS detectors sit in the cabin air return vents and wait for the ventilation to bring smoke to them.
rules.verdictRule: Holds at 0 g as ISS design practice. Unknown in partial gravity: NASA says smoke transport there is unclear and only models exist.

rules.rule: Stop the airflow and the fire goes out
rules.issPractice: The first response to a fire in microgravity is to turn off forced airflow. BASS results on the station supported that protocol.
rules.verdictRule: Breaks in partial gravity, where NASA says natural convection keeps feeding the fire. Breaks at 0 g from 26.5% oxygen, where station burner tests held steady flames in still gas. Weakens at 0 g below that, where some Saffire fuels kept burning without flow.

rules.rule: A narrow gap smothers a flame
rules.issPractice: On the station a flame squeezed between two surfaces stops spreading once the gap is tight enough.
rules.verdictRule: Holds at 0 g, measured on the station, with a caveat about intermediate gaps. Breaks in partial gravity, where NASA expects a chimney effect.

rules.rule: A CO₂ extinguisher can be emptied into the cabin
rules.issPractice: The ISS US segment was equipped with portable CO₂ extinguishers holding 2.7 kg of gas.
rules.verdictRule: Calculated: one 2.7 kg discharge, mixed through the cabin. Breaks above 30.4 mmHg of CO₂, the NIOSH immediate-danger level at sea-level pressure. Otherwise weakens, because NASA already replaced the units on the ISS over crew exposure.

rules.rule: The crew can breathe from oxygen masks
rules.issPractice: ISS crews are told to put on emergency masks that supply pure oxygen when smoke builds up.
rules.verdictRule: Breaks at or below 19.6 m³, the pressurized volume of Orion, where NASA says mask oxygen would enrich the cabin. Holds at ISS scale, 388 m³ and above. Unknown in between: no published threshold.

rules.rule: The cabin dilutes smoke and gases to tolerable levels
rules.issPractice: A large station spreads combustion products through a large volume. Saffire tested what the same kind of fire does in 17 to 19 m³.
rules.verdictRule: Calculated: the largest Saffire VI gas release, rescaled to this cabin. Breaks above the 425 ppm one-hour CO limit. Weakens above the 100 ppm 24-hour CO limit or the 3 mmHg one-hour CO₂ limit. Otherwise holds.

rules.rule: Emergency resupply and a ride home are close
rules.issPractice: ISS fire protocols lean on contingency resupply and on docked vehicles that can bring the crew home.
rules.verdictRule: Programme context, not combustion data. Holds in low Earth orbit. Breaks beyond it.

verdicts.explanation: Station experiments show flames surviving at lower oxygen in microgravity than in the 1 g test. A pass on the ground is not a worst case.

On the station the detector stayed silent for Kapton smoke in half of the tests and for Teflon smoke in two-thirds. Both plastics are widely used in electronics, the most likely source of fire and smoke in a spacecraft.
Station air is clean, yet suspended dust still causes nuisance alarms and crews switch detectors off while vacuuming. This cabin is assumed to use the same kind of detector.
Without buoyancy the ventilation is the only thing moving smoke, so detectors in the return vents see it. Detection is slower than on Earth.

Small samples on the station went out quickly once the flow stopped. On Saffire IV a thick acrylic slab stayed alight through 15 s without flow, kept going by its own jets of fuel vapour. The Saffire authors conclude that quick extinction cannot be assumed in still conditions.

verdicts.reason: Flame fails below a limiting gap
verdicts.explanation: Station tests found a limiting gap below which the flame fails to spread. The same tests found the fastest spread at an intermediate gap, so a moderately tight space can burn faster than a wider one.

One 2.7 kg discharge mixed through 1,005 m³ gives 1.1 mmHg of CO₂, about 0.15% of the cabin gas. The one-hour limit is 3 mmHg and the immediate-danger level is about 30 mmHg. Station emergency breathing equipment does not filter CO₂, a concern NASA cites for the move to water mist. Near the nozzle the level is higher than this cabin average.

This is station practice. In a volume this large the oxygen released by masks changes the cabin level very little. In this cabin about 11,881 standard litres of released oxygen lift the oxygen level by one percentage point.

The Saffire VI acrylic fire, about 1.3 MJ, would raise carbon monoxide by 2.8 ppm and CO₂ by 0.06 mmHg in this cabin if perfectly mixed. Limits: 100 ppm CO for 24 hours, 425 ppm for one hour, 3 mmHg CO₂ for one hour. Near the fire the levels are higher than this cabin average.
In low Earth orbit the protocols can count on contingency resupply and on docked vehicles for leaving the station.

verdicts.reason: Flame fails below a limiting gap
verdicts.explanation: Station tests found a limiting gap below which the flame fails to spread. The same tests found the fastest spread at an intermediate gap, so a moderately tight space can burn faster than a wider one.

One 2.7 kg discharge mixed through 9.3 m³ gives 122 mmHg of CO₂, about 14% of the cabin gas. The one-hour limit is 3 mmHg and the immediate-danger level is about 30 mmHg. The extinguisher itself becomes the hazard.

NASA judged the ISS breathing apparatus unsuitable for Orion, because in so small a volume the oxygen fed to the crew raises the cabin oxygen level and feeds the fire. This cabin is no larger than Orion. In this cabin about 110 standard litres of released oxygen lift the oxygen level by one percentage point.

The Saffire VI acrylic fire, about 1.3 MJ, would raise carbon monoxide by 298 ppm and CO₂ by 6.3 mmHg in this cabin if perfectly mixed. Limits: 100 ppm CO for 24 hours, 425 ppm for one hour, 3 mmHg CO₂ for one hour.

A published review of spacecraft fire safety notes that deep-space expeditions have no emergency resupply and must be more self-reliant. Response resources used up on one fire leave the crew exposed to a second accident.
Ground tests at lunar gravity found materials burning at oxygen levels where the normal-gravity test passes them. At 34% oxygen the margin shrinks further.

verdicts.basis: Measured in orbit, carried over from 0 g
verdicts.explanation: On the station the detector stayed silent for Kapton smoke in half of the tests and for Teflon smoke in two-thirds. Both plastics are widely used in electronics, the most likely source of fire and smoke in a spacecraft. Smoke from overheated materials has not been measured in partial gravity, so this result is carried over from orbit.

Chamber tests with lunar regolith simulant show smoke and dust overlapping in particle size and setting off the detector. NASA states that a lunar detection system has to tell combustion particles from cabin dust and lunar dust.

With some gravity a weak buoyant smoke plume competes with the ventilation flow. NASA modelling for lunar gravity expects the two to be of similar strength. There are computer models but no measurements, and NASA has not settled whether detectors belong on the ceiling or at the air intakes.

With some gravity, hot gas rises and pulls fresh air in after it, fans or no fans. NASA Glenn states that stopping ventilation is not an effective way to put out a fire in lunar or Martian gravity. Station burner tests also held steady flames in still gas at 26.5% oxygen and above, and this cabin runs at 34%.
With gravity present a gap behaves like a chimney. NASA Glenn states that buoyant flow can drive a fire inside a small space in partial gravity.

One 2.7 kg discharge mixed through 17 m³ gives 67 mmHg of CO₂, about 14% of the cabin gas. The one-hour limit is 3 mmHg and the immediate-danger level is about 30 mmHg. The extinguisher itself becomes the hazard.

NASA judged the ISS breathing apparatus unsuitable for Orion, because in so small a volume the oxygen fed to the crew raises the cabin oxygen level and feeds the fire. This cabin is no larger than Orion. In this cabin about 135 standard litres of released oxygen lift the oxygen level by one percentage point.

evidence.conditions: ISS glovebox, cotton and fibreglass fabric, airflow against the flame, station air
evidence.finding: The fabric held a flame spreading against the airflow. In normal-gravity air the matching downward spread goes out by itself.
evidence.source: NASA Glenn and USRA. Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) results slides. NTRS 20130012832.

evidence.conditions: ISS, acrylic samples, oxygen and pressure varied
evidence.finding: The team reports a flammability limit near 15% oxygen on the station against roughly 18% in normal gravity. They note that airflow speed or gravity could be the cause.
evidence.source: UC Berkeley Research. NASA-Funded Project Offers New Insights Into Fire Behavior in Space. 9 December 2024.

evidence.conditions: NASA Glenn research summary
evidence.finding: A microgravity flame is weaker than a 1 g flame, yet it keeps spreading at lower oxygen percentages.
evidence.source: Urban, D. (NASA Glenn). Update on NASA Materials Flammability Research. 7th FLARE International Workshop, September 2021. NTRS 20210021181.

evidence.conditions: Centrifuge inside the NASA Glenn 5.2 s drop tower, three thin materials, lunar gravity
evidence.finding: All three materials burned at lower oxygen concentrations in lunar gravity than in normal gravity. The authors caution that the short test time changes the limit criteria.
evidence.source: Ferkul, P. V., Olson, S. L. Zero-gravity centrifuge used for the evaluation of material flammability in Lunar gravity. Journal of Thermophysics and Heat Transfer 25(3), 457–461 (2011).

evidence.conditions: Nomex, Mylar and Ultem 1000 at zero, lunar, Martian and normal gravity
evidence.finding: At the highest oxygen level each material passes in normal gravity, flames still spread in partial gravity for all three. Lunar gravity can give a lower limit than zero or Martian gravity, and the trend depends on the material.
evidence.source: Urban, D. (NASA Glenn). Update on NASA Materials Flammability Research. 7th FLARE International Workshop, September 2021. NTRS 20210021181.

evidence.conditions: Cotton and fibreglass fabric in air, lunar gravity from a drop-tower centrifuge and parabolic flight
evidence.finding: The fabric burns downward in lunar gravity. In Earth gravity it goes out right after ignition.
evidence.source: Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2). NASA Glenn and USRA, 2024. NTRS 20240015307.

evidence.conditions: NASA and USRA summary, March 2026
evidence.finding: Evidence is mounting that a material which passes the standard test can fail below 1 g. Models and experiments point to lunar gravity as close to the most flammable condition.
evidence.source: Ferkul, P., Kralik, N., Liao, Y.-T., Johnston, M. Material Flammability at Lunar and Martian Gravity. Lunar and Planetary Science Conference, March 2026. NTRS 20260001966.

evidence.conditions: Apollo 1 ground test, 1967, cabin pressurized with 100% oxygen
evidence.finding: The fire spread quickly in the pure oxygen atmosphere. Afterwards NASA severely restricted and controlled the combustible materials allowed in the cabin.
evidence.source: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance. Apollo 1.

evidence.conditions: ISS glovebox, smoke from overheated Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, cellulose and Pyrell
evidence.finding: The ISS detector failed to alarm for Kapton smoke in half of the tests and for Teflon smoke in two-thirds.
evidence.source: Fortenberry, C., Wang, X., Cleary, T., et al. Research Questions and Challenges for Improved Spacecraft Fire Detection. White paper for the Biological and Physical Sciences Decadal Survey, 2021. NTRS 20210022143.

evidence.conditions: Same experiment, ISS light-scattering detector and Shuttle ionization detector side by side
evidence.finding: Neither detector caught every smoke type. Large particles from cellulose, silicone and Pyrell were picked up easily, while the smaller Teflon and Kapton particles were often missed. Both plastics are common in electronics.
evidence.source: NIST. NIST/NASA Study Shows One Detector Doesn’t “Fit All” for Smoke in Spacecraft. News release, 1 May 2018.

evidence.conditions: Same experiment, journal paper
evidence.finding: The two spacecraft smoke detectors did not detect every type of smoke. Particles made on the station were not significantly different from those made in matching ground tests.
evidence.source: Meyer, M., Urban, D., Mulholland, G., et al. Evaluation of spacecraft smoke detector performance in the low-gravity environment. Fire Safety Journal 98 (2018) 74.

evidence.conditions: Saffire VI, Cygnus with 16.7 m³ free volume
evidence.finding: Smoke at the far-field sensor unit reached the alarm threshold at 981 s. By then much of the hazardous gas had been released.
evidence.source: Urban, D. L., Ruff, G. A., Ferkul, P., et al. Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment. ICES-2024-365. NTRS 20240002981.

evidence.conditions: NASA and USRA poster, 2023
evidence.finding: Smoke particle properties under partial gravity, elevated oxygen and reduced pressure are listed as ongoing and future measurements.
evidence.source: Fortenberry, C., Balasubramaniam, R., Urban, D. The Influence of Smoke Particle Properties and Cabin Characteristics on Smoke Detection in Lunar Gravity. AAAR 41st Annual Conference, 2023, poster. NTRS 20230013826.

evidence.conditions: ISS cabin air sampled with a particle counter and a dust monitor
evidence.finding: Cabin air averaged about 0.005 mg/m³ and 15 particles per cm³, substantially cleaner than the Shuttle or a typical office.
evidence.source: Urban, D., Ruff, G., Sheredy, W., Funk, G. Particle and Smoke Detection on ISS for Next Generation Smoke Detectors. International Space Development Conference, 2007. NTRS 20070031686.

evidence.conditions: ISS operations
evidence.finding: The ISS detector does not select for smoke particles, so suspended dust causes nuisance alarms. Crews typically disable the detectors while vacuuming.
evidence.source: Fortenberry, C., Wang, X., Cleary, T., et al. Research Questions and Challenges for Improved Spacecraft Fire Detection. White paper for the Biological and Physical Sciences Decadal Survey, 2021. NTRS 20210022143.

evidence.conditions: NASA Glenn technology summary
evidence.finding: Habitat maintenance can release particles and cause false fire alarms.
evidence.source: Ruff, G. A. (NASA Glenn). Development of Spacecraft Fire Safety Technology for Exploration. FLARE Workshop, September 2021. NTRS 20210021318.

evidence.conditions: NASA Glenn chamber tests with a lunar highlands regolith simulant
evidence.finding: Smoke and lunar dust have overlapping particle sizes that set off the detector. NASA states that the detection system has to tell combustion particles from cabin dust and lunar dust.
evidence.source: NASA Glenn Research Center. Early Fire Detection System for Partial and Low Gravity Environments. 2026. NTRS 20260005612.

evidence.conditions: Fire detector described by NASA Spinoff in 1978
evidence.finding: A detector that samples the air for combustion particles can tell them from dust, which makes it less susceptible to false alarms.
evidence.source: NASA Spinoff 1978. Fire Detector.

evidence.conditions: ISS design
evidence.finding: Microgravity has no buoyant smoke plume, so ISS detectors sit in the cabin air return vents ahead of the filters and the ventilation brings the smoke to them.
evidence.source: Fortenberry, C., Wang, X., Cleary, T., et al. Research Questions and Challenges for Improved Spacecraft Fire Detection. White paper for the Biological and Physical Sciences Decadal Survey, 2021. NTRS 20210022143.

evidence.conditions: NASA and NIST smoke transport study
evidence.finding: Detection takes longer than in normal gravity.
evidence.source: Urban, D. L., Ruff, G. A., Brooker, J. E., et al. Spacecraft Fire Detection: Smoke Properties and Transport in Low-Gravity. NTRS 20080012612.

evidence.conditions: NASA Glenn research summary
evidence.finding: It is unclear how limited buoyancy will move smoke. Modelling is needed to choose between ceiling detectors and detectors at floor-level air intakes.
evidence.source: Urban, D. (NASA Glenn). Update on NASA Materials Flammability Research. 7th FLARE International Workshop, September 2021. NTRS 20210021181.

evidence.conditions: Computer model of a 2 m cabin volume in lunar gravity
evidence.finding: Buoyant and forced flow are expected to be of similar size. A smoke layer partly survives at 1 cm/s of forced flow and is mixed through the volume at 5 cm/s. Where to put detectors stays an open question.
evidence.source: Fortenberry, C., Balasubramaniam, R., Urban, D. The Influence of Smoke Particle Properties and Cabin Characteristics on Smoke Detection in Lunar Gravity. AAAR 41st Annual Conference, 2023, poster. NTRS 20230013826.

evidence.conditions: NASA Glenn technology summary
evidence.finding: In partial gravity smoke production, buoyancy and life-support air circulation compete. Lunar gravity can change the detection strategy depending on vehicle design.
evidence.source: Ruff, G. A. (NASA Glenn). Development of Spacecraft Fire Safety Technology for Exploration. FLARE Workshop, September 2021. NTRS 20210021318.

evidence.conditions: ISS glovebox, station air
evidence.finding: After two minutes of burning the airflow was switched off and the flame went out rapidly.
evidence.source: NASA Tech Briefs. ISS Experiment Studies Flames and Fire Suppression in Space. 1 October 2012.

evidence.conditions: ISS glovebox, 0.1 mm thick sample, airflow against the flame
evidence.finding: The flame quenched when the flow fell below about 2 cm/s and neared blow-off as it passed 40 cm/s.
evidence.source: Combustion of Solids in Microgravity: Results from the BASS-II Experiment. NTRS 20160000593.

evidence.conditions: ISS, 25 mm gas burner emulating solid and liquid fuels, no forced flow
evidence.finding: Every flame at 21% oxygen went out by itself within 40 s.
evidence.source: Dehghani, P. Burning Emulations of Condensed Phase Fuels Aboard the International Space Station. University of Maryland, 2022.

evidence.conditions: Saffire IV, Cygnus, acrylic slab burning on two sides, 100 kPa, 22% oxygen
evidence.finding: When the fan was cut the hot sample kept bubbling, and its jets of fuel vapour stirred enough mixing to keep the flame alive through 15 s without flow.
evidence.source: Urban, D. L., Ruff, G. A., Ferkul, P., et al. Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires. ICES-2021-266. NTRS 20210011521.

evidence.conditions: Saffire V, Cygnus, cotton jersey, 70.7 kPa, 26.2% oxygen
evidence.finding: With the fan off for about 70 s, glowing embers and small blue flamelets remained. The flame grew back when the flow returned and burned about 150 s more.
evidence.source: Urban, D. L., Ruff, G. A., Ferkul, P., et al. Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires. ICES-2021-266. NTRS 20210011521.

evidence.conditions: Saffire V, acrylic samples, 71 to 73 kPa, about 25.5% oxygen
evidence.finding: After 300 s at 5 cm/s the fan was turned off and both samples went out immediately. The authors still conclude that extinction cannot be assumed to come quickly in still conditions.
evidence.source: Urban, D. L., Ruff, G. A., Ferkul, P., et al. Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires. ICES-2021-266. NTRS 20210011521.

evidence.conditions: ISS, 25 mm gas burner emulating solid and liquid fuels, no forced flow
evidence.finding: Steady flames were observed at 26.5, 34 and 40% oxygen.
evidence.source: Dehghani, P. Burning Emulations of Condensed Phase Fuels Aboard the International Space Station. University of Maryland, 2022.

evidence.conditions: NASA Glenn research summary
evidence.finding: Stopping the ventilation flow is not an effective way to put out a fire in lunar or Martian gravity, because natural convection keeps supplying air.
evidence.source: Urban, D. (NASA Glenn). Update on NASA Materials Flammability Research. 7th FLARE International Workshop, September 2021. NTRS 20210021181.

evidence.conditions: Community white paper
evidence.finding: The lack of direct tests in partial gravity is called troubling, because available results suggest lunar and Martian gravity could make flame spread more likely.
evidence.source: Gollner, M., Wichman, I. S., Liao, Y.-T., Carmignani, L., et al. Solid Fuel Combustion in Partial and Micro-Gravity. Topical white paper, 2021. NTRS 20210022402.

evidence.conditions: ISS glovebox, thin fabric burning between two baffles in forced flow
evidence.finding: Below a limiting distance between the baffles the flame fails to spread.
evidence.source: Li, Y., Liao, Y.-T. T., Ferkul, P. V., Johnston, M. C., Bunnell, C. Experimental study of concurrent-flow flame spread over thin solids in confined space in microgravity. Combustion and Flame 227 (2021) 39–51. Conference version: NTRS 20205004657.

evidence.conditions: Same experiment
evidence.finding: Spread rate and flame length peak at an intermediate gap. Confinement speeds up the flow and reflects heat back, until short oxygen supply and heat loss to the walls take over.
evidence.source: Li, Y., Liao, Y.-T. T., Ferkul, P. V., Johnston, M. C., Bunnell, C. Experimental study of concurrent-flow flame spread over thin solids in confined space in microgravity. Combustion and Flame 227 (2021) 39–51. Conference version: NTRS 20205004657.

evidence.conditions: NASA Glenn research summary
evidence.finding: In partial gravity buoyant flow can drive a fire inside a small space, a chimney effect.
evidence.source: Urban, D. (NASA Glenn). Update on NASA Materials Flammability Research. 7th FLARE International Workshop, September 2021. NTRS 20210021181.

evidence.conditions: ISS operations
evidence.finding: Station emergency breathing equipment does not filter carbon dioxide, which NASA calls a serious concern. Nine water-mist extinguishers were built to replace the original CO₂ units, and the last one reached the station in 2016.
evidence.source: NASA Spinoff 2020. Zero-Leak Valve Holds Tight in Demanding Environments.

evidence.conditions: ISS, heptane and methanol droplets, CO₂ dispersed into air at 1 atm
evidence.finding: Steady droplet burning stopped only once the gas reached about 17% oxygen with 20% CO₂ for heptane, and 14% oxygen with 30% CO₂ for methanol.
evidence.source: Dietrich, D. L., Nayagam, V., Hicks, M. C., et al. Droplet Combustion Experiments Aboard the International Space Station. Microgravity Science and Technology 26, 65–76 (2014).

evidence.conditions: ISS US segment equipment
evidence.finding: The portable CO₂ extinguishers hold 2.7 kg of gas compressed to 58 atm.
evidence.source: Guibaud, A., Legros, G., Consalvi, J.-L., Torero, J. Fire safety in spacecraft: past incidents and Deep Space challenges. Acta Astronautica, author manuscript at UCL Discovery.

evidence.conditions: NASA Glenn technology summary
evidence.finding: Orion carries a water-mist extinguisher.
evidence.source: Ruff, G. A. (NASA Glenn). Development of Spacecraft Fire Safety Technology for Exploration. FLARE Workshop, September 2021. NTRS 20210021318.

evidence.conditions: Mir, 24 February 1997, burning solid-fuel oxygen generator
evidence.finding: Three foam extinguishers were used on the flame, which lasted several minutes and finally went out by itself.
evidence.source: Uri, J. 25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir. NASA History, 23 February 2022.

evidence.conditions: ISS procedure
evidence.finding: Crews are told to put on emergency masks that supply pure oxygen when smoke builds up.
evidence.source: Guibaud, A., Legros, G., Consalvi, J.-L., Torero, J. Fire safety in spacecraft: past incidents and Deep Space challenges. Acta Astronautica, author manuscript at UCL Discovery.

evidence.conditions: NASA Glenn technology summary, Orion
evidence.finding: The ISS breathing apparatus does not suit Orion. In so small a volume the oxygen given to the crew would raise the cabin oxygen level and add to the fire risk. Water mist could also film over the ISS mask filter.
evidence.source: Ruff, G. A. (NASA Glenn). Development of Spacecraft Fire Safety Technology for Exploration. FLARE Workshop, September 2021. NTRS 20210021318.

evidence.conditions: NASA capability gap list
evidence.finding: NASA lists an emergency crew mask that is compatible with small cabin volumes and adds no oxygen to the cabin.
evidence.source: Ruff, G. A. (NASA Glenn). Spacecraft Fire Safety Systems Maturation Team Status. 2016, hosted by the National Academies.

evidence.conditions: Mir, 24 February 1997, six crew members aboard
evidence.finding: The crew quickly put on oxygen masks. The station life support system cleared the smoke over the next several hours.
evidence.source: Uri, J. 25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir. NASA History, 23 February 2022.

evidence.conditions: Saffire VI, Cygnus with 16.7 m³ free volume, 54 to 55 kPa, 29 to 30% oxygen, two acrylic fires releasing 1,280 and 830 kJ
evidence.finding: Carbon monoxide at the far-field inlet rose by 308 and 320 ppm and CO₂ by 3.51 and 3.37 mmHg. Both fires passed the 3 mmHg one-hour CO₂ limit. CO was well above the 100 ppm 24-hour limit and close to the 425 ppm one-hour limit.
evidence.source: Urban, D. L., Ruff, G. A., Ferkul, P., et al. Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment. ICES-2024-365. NTRS 20240002981.

evidence.conditions: Saffire IV to VI, fires of 1.5 to 3.2 kW in 17 to 19 m³ of free volume
evidence.finding: Temperature and pressure rise mattered less than the rise in carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide.
evidence.source: Urban, D. L., Ruff, G. A., Ferkul, P., et al. Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment. ICES-2024-365. NTRS 20240002981.

evidence.conditions: Saffire IV and V, prototype smoke eater with a CO oxidation catalyst and activated carbon
evidence.finding: Little carbon monoxide was removed during the burns. The cause was still under investigation, with catalyst fouling and bed packing as suspects.
evidence.source: Fortenberry, C., Casteel, M., Graf, J., et al. Evaluation of Combustion Products from Large-Scale Spacecraft Fires during the Saffire-IV and Saffire-V Experiments. ICES 2021, presentation. NTRS 20210017343.

evidence.conditions: Saffire VI conclusions
evidence.finding: Extending these results to the partial gravity of the Moon and Mars needs further work.
evidence.source: Urban, D. L., Ruff, G. A., Ferkul, P., et al. Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment. ICES-2024-365. NTRS 20240002981.

evidence.conditions: Review of spacecraft fire incidents and protocols
evidence.finding: ISS protocols lean on contingency resupply and on the crew being able to leave in docked return vehicles.
evidence.source: Guibaud, A., Legros, G., Consalvi, J.-L., Torero, J. Fire safety in spacecraft: past incidents and Deep Space challenges. Acta Astronautica, author manuscript at UCL Discovery.

evidence.conditions: Mir, 24 February 1997, six crew members and two docked Soyuz vehicles
evidence.finding: The flame blocked the evacuation route to one of the two Soyuz spacecraft.
evidence.source: Uri, J. 25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir. NASA History, 23 February 2022.

evidence.conditions: Apollo 13, on the way to the Moon
evidence.finding: When an oxygen tank blew up on the third day of the flight, the crew moved into the lunar module and used it as a lifeboat until splashdown.
evidence.source: NASA Office of Safety and Mission Assurance. Apollo 13.

evidence.conditions: Review of spacecraft fire incidents and protocols
evidence.finding: Deep-space expeditions have no emergency resupply, and lunar and Martian plans call for more self-reliance. A fire that uses up the response resources leaves the crew exposed to a second accident.
evidence.source: Guibaud, A., Legros, G., Consalvi, J.-L., Torero, J. Fire safety in spacecraft: past incidents and Deep Space challenges. Acta Astronautica, author manuscript at UCL Discovery.
